subject_line: Leonora Gelb and the Peru of The Gringa
email_body:
Dear Andrew,

The Gringa sets Leonora Gelb, an American who spends years in a Peruvian prison, inside long passages of Peruvian history, so her story is never the only one on the page.

I'd love to ask how you settled the balance between Leonora's chapters and the history around her.

book_title: The After-Normal: Brief, Alphabetical Essays on a Changing Planet
subject_line: Why the alphabet, in The After-Normal
email_body:
Dear Nicole,

The After-Normal sets its brief essays on a changing planet in alphabetical order, which gives a book about uncertainty an oddly calm, almost dictionary-like spine. In an older Essay Daily conversation you spoke about Flagstaff's ravens and vultures finding their way into your writing.

I'd love to ask how the alphabetical form came about, and whether it made the subject easier or harder to face.

subject_line: Karl Hofer and the sequence in Early Hour
email_body:
Dear Michael,

Early Hour caught my attention as a book-length sequence drawn from the work of Karl Hofer, the German Expressionist painter persecuted by the Nazis. It is a long way from the Coos Bay landscapes reviewers heard in Home Burial, yet it still feels like your voice.

I'd like to ask how you first came to Hofer's paintings, and what writing a single sequence allowed you to do.

subject_line: The office in Orientation, years later
email_body:
Dear Daniel,

The title story of Orientation and Other Stories, a new-hire tour of an office built from snapshots of its employees, was your first published story, and I read that it came after about a decade of office work around the Bay Area.

I'd love to ask how those years turned into satire, and whether you still recognise that office in the story when you reread it now.

subject_line: From Here, Bullet to Phantom Noise
email_body:
Dear Brian,

Here, Bullet chronicles your time in Iraq, yet it is not only a book of combat poems, and Phantom Noise, later shortlisted for the T.S. Eliot Prize, seemed to follow that war home. I'd like to ask, with My Life as a Foreign Country in mind too, how returning to the same years in different forms has changed what you see in them, and how that shapes your teaching in the Nevada low-residency MFA you founded.
